text:
Understanding

Two Types of Next.js Components: 1) Server and 2) Client

The key idea and difference is: where the code runs not when
Server components

The JS runs on the Next.js Server to produce HTML
In hybrid/SSR Next.js this could be in the actual Next.js server in real-time in production as there is a server
In export/SSG Next.js this runs on Next.js during build time to produce HTML that is deploy to a serverless static site host.

Client Components

The Next.js code (JS) is shipped and runs in the clients browser


Best practice is to user Server Compoents; ‘use client’ only when required on smaller niche compoentns that need it

title: Line endings on four axes: LF vs CRLF, repo vs local, .gitattributes, and the refresh
text:
2. Understanding

Triage

There are some core concepts i need to understand (LF vs CRLF)
then there is tooling around these that are secondary
lets start with the concepts
then move on to the tooling



2.1 Core Concept: OS newline or End of Line (EOL) conventions

When a line of code ends; there are are two ways of ending the line when it comes to the binary aspect - way 1 and way 2
Way 1 amd way 2 are not rules. they can both work on tools acoss operating systems (windows git vs mac/unix git)
But each tool-os has their defaults

Windows git defaults to way 1
Unix/Mac git defaults to way 2

History of way 1 and way 2

a bit is a binary digit 0 or 1
a byte is a 8 bits
most ASCII characters (aka most of code) is 1 byte per character
There are two characters that are using in encoding end of line

Line Feed (LF) aka \n  
Carriage Return (CR) aka \r
historically these came from typewriters; where to type a new line you needed to type both to create the new line in typewriters
When people started writing code on computers (keyboards) not type-writers
we didn’t need both to encode a new line but the two branches fork a bit in terms of opinion

Unix/Mac - we dont need both so lets jsut simplfiy and keep one LF (one less byte per line! - without losing anyhting other than deviation from history)
Windows - said lets keep the old traditional at the end of line type both the CR + LF - (\r \n) like typewriters did



The problem 

Prettier standardizes to test that the code base sohuld be LF  (Unix/Mac)
but our windows tooling often produces CRLFleading to frequent prettier failures

title: Line endings on four axes: LF vs CRLF, repo vs local, .gitattributes, and the refresh
text:
2.2 Tooling

So now we are on to the tooling (speiccally github). There three thigns i want to udnrestand

.gitattribute (specifically the EOL config)
implications for local vs remote
how the recommended fix command works  git rm -r --cached -q :/ && git reset --hard

GitHub remote/cloud/origin stores  on the cloud a version of your codebase including the EOL - the commited bytes
Git has a sepcific file called   .gitattirbutes which stores the configurations for how git converts and works with your codebase (e..g on clones or commits); one such config is the EOL config
So to fix the preittier warning/bug; the first step is to always make sure your gitattribute EOL config is set to LF and Commit/push
But what the config is set in the gitattrbute is not teh same as what bytes (EOL) are saved in the github repo origin and local. These stored byte vs LF config in gittatrbutes can exist in two scenarios
There can be two cases where we can have the bad EOL (CRLF)

Case one its on the GitHub Repo in the cloud/origin - Repo CRLF
Case 2 the Repo is okay its Repo LF but local CRLF

These two cases have two fixes

Case 1 Repo CRLF

we can call git add --renormalize which will re-appled the settings of LF in .gitattributes to every tracekd file, so CRLF gets stroed as LF on the next commit and push

Case 2 Repo LF but Local CRLF

we can call ``git rm -r –cached -q :/ && git reset –hard`` 
Whihc does the following

git rm -r --cached -q :/ empties the index; disk untouched
git reset --hard rebuilds the index and rewrites every file through .gitattributes, as LF
risk is that this discards uncommitted edits. so make sure you run this on a clean worktree!

title: Line endings on four axes: LF vs CRLF, repo vs local, .gitattributes, and the refresh
text:
a. Diff LF vs CRLF
The same two lines of code, saved with each line ending. ␍ is CR (\r) and ␊ is LF (\n); both are normally invisible.
- const a = 1;␍␊      ← CRLF (Windows): 2 bytes per line ending
- const b = 2;␍␊
+ const a = 1;␊        ← LF (Unix/Mac): 1 byte per line ending
+ const b = 2;␊
Raw bytes (od -c):
- c o n s t   a   =   1 ; \r \n
+ c o n s t   a   =   1 ; \n
The text is identical. The only difference is the extra \r before every \n.
Prettier (default endOfLine: "lf") flags each of those \r characters:
1:13  error  Delete `␍`  prettier/prettier

Details/References

Common triggers
Docs: Events that trigger workflows








Trigger
Fires when
Example use

Commits land on a branch or tag
Deploy on merge to main

A PR is opened or updated
Test or render before merge


workflow_dispatch
Someone clicks “Run workflow” (or runs gh workflow run)
Manual redeploy

A cron time is reached
Nightly data refresh


release
A release is published
Publish a package


workflow_call
Another workflow calls this one
Reusable build steps



Note: main is not a trigger on its own. It is push plus a branches: [main] filter.


Filters
Docs: Using filters, branches, paths








Filter
Narrows by
Works on

Branch name
push, pull_request (the PR’s target branch)

Tag name
push

Files changed
push, pull_request

Activity type (e.g. opened, closed)
pull_request, release, issues


cron
Time

inputs
Values passed at launch
workflow_dispatch, workflow_call



Note: paths does not work on workflow_dispatch or schedule.


Job-level control
Docs: jobs.<job_id>.if, jobs.<job_id>.needs, Status check functions, jobs.<job_id>.environment








Control
What it does
Example




if:
Runs the job only when a condition is true
if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'


needs:
Waits for other jobs; skipped if one fails
needs: build


if: success()
Runs when every needed job passed (the default)
Deploy after tests pass


if: failure()
Runs only when a needed job failed
Send an alert


if: always()
Runs no matter what
Cleanup

Waits for an approval or protection rule
Manual sign-off before deploy

1. Agent Bullet Points (make a toggle colabspoible later)
Part 1: R installations

User mode: installs R without admin rights
Portable Linux builds run on any glibc/musl distro
rig rtools installs and manages Rtools on Windows
Sets up RStudio and Positron automatically
P3M is now the default; new repos add and status
User mode is less tested than admin mode

Part 2: R packages (rig pkg)

Installs packages like pak, without starting R
Sources: CRAN, GitHub, git, URLs, local paths
Version constraints: @==, ^, ~
Dependency solver, parallel downloads, shared cache
doctor finds broken or missing dependencies
info, deps, tree, search look up packages
Installs system deps automatically on major Linux distros
The rig website labels it experimental

Part 3: R projects (rig proj)

Works like uv or cargo: rproj.toml plus rproj.lock
One lockfile covers several platforms and R versions
Locked versions stay put until you --upgrade
sync builds .rvenv and installs R if missing
Projects share package files on disk, so libraries are cheap
rig run runs project code or inline-dependency scripts
Imports a project from DESCRIPTION or renv.lock
devtools and similar tools live in a shared tools library
The rig website labels it experimental

text: Terms follow the Claude Code docs (commands). Terms that are not official are marked informal. Behaviors confirmed by hand are marked tested and link to the tidbit that tested them.

title: Claude Code
text:
Session







Term
Meaning




session
One open Claude Code window, holding one conversation


context
What Claude remembers in this session. /clear wipes it


turn
One round: you send → Claude works → Claude replies. A turn is made of tool calls and reading any text you typed in the meantime. A skill call always starts a new turn


busy / idle (informal)
Busy = a turn is running. Idle = no turn running. A background tool call does not keep Claude busy

title: Claude Code
text:
Tool calls



Term
Meaning




tool call
One action inside a turn (Bash, Read, Edit, …). A turn can have many


foreground tool call
The default. The turn waits for it to finish, so Claude stays busy. To force it, say “wait for it”


background tool call
Runs on its own, outside the turn; the turn ends without it, so Claude is idle. A Bash command goes to the background when you ask, when you press Ctrl+B, when it times out, or when it is banned in the foreground (e.g. sleep)


AskUserQuestion
A tool call that asks you something and does not finish until you answer. The turn stays busy while the question is pending (tested, tidbit)

title: Claude Code
text:
Commands







Term
Meaning




slash command
Anything typed as /something. Either a built-in (/clear, /compact, /model) or a skill from a plugin or the user (/dev-log)


skill
A custom slash command defined in a plugin or .claude/skills. Running one starts a new turn

title: Claude Code
text:
Typing while Claude works
Two questions decide what happens to anything you type:

Is Claude busy? Busy = a turn is running. Idle = no turn running. A background tool call does not count; a pending AskUserQuestion does.
What did you type? Plain text, or a slash command.










Text
Slash command




Idle
runs now
runs now


Busy
joins the current turn, at the next gap between tool calls
waits; runs after the turn ends



So mid-turn, text always runs before a queued slash command, whatever order you typed them.



Term
Meaning




queue
One list of everything you typed mid-turn, in the order you typed it


text, queued
Handed to Claude at the next gap between tool calls, inside the current turn. So it is answered before the turn ends, and before any queued slash command — whatever order you typed them (tested, tidbit)


slash command, queued
Waits in the list and runs after the current turn ends, as its own step. A pending AskUserQuestion keeps the turn alive, so a queued /clear waits for your answer (tested, tidbit)


text, during a pending question
Taken as the answer to the question, not queued (tested, tidbit)


immediate commands
A few built-ins never queue: /status, /tasks, /usage


send now
Ctrl+Enter or Ctrl+X Ctrl+S sends queued input right away instead of waiting. Up from an empty input box takes queued items back into the box

title: Proof of Concept: Client-side Serverless DuckDB query of cloud bucket storages
text:
Intro
This demonstrates a serverless analytics stack combining Static Site Generation (SSG) with cloud-hosted Parquet datasets via DuckDB WASM. This architecture enables lightweight, cost-effective deployment of static site front ends with integration to cloud data stroage (S3 or other databases) using client-side SQL processing via DuckDB WASM.
Use Cases:

Interactive dashboards deployed to CDNs
Real-time analytics on static hosting (Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages)
Client-side data processing without API costs
Scalable data visualization with minimal infrastructure

Architecture Benefits:

Zero server costs (static hosting only)
Automatic global CDN distribution
Direct cloud dataset access
Client-side SQL processing



Data Source (Hugging Faces Parquet)
We access Parquet files from Hugging Face, an open-science repository with ML-optimized APIs and CORS-enabled endpoints suitable for browser-based applications. However this workflow works with any storage provider (Azure, AWS, GCP, Hugging Face, etc.). We use Hugging Face because it’s a gold standard open-science data repository that is performant and free.


Traditional Server-side Pattern (R/Python/Node.js running on server)
We can query as we do normally working on a local or cloud comptuer that is running some server; in this case its R code but it could be any language the query syntax is native SQL.

library(duckdb); library(tidyverse)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

result <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT * 
  FROM 'https://huggingface.co/datasets/ran-codes/mtcars/resolve/refs%2Fconvert%2Fparquet/default/train/0000.parquet' 
") |> as_tibble()

result |> glimpse()

Columns: 12

$ carb  <dbl> 4, 4, 1, 1, 2, 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2…

Serverless/Client-side Pattern (WASM running in browser)
DuckDB WASM enables SQL processing directly in browsers, eliminating server dependencies. Below is the serverless equivalent of the query from above.
Let’s first import DuckDB WASM from npm (Javascript package manager).

// Import DuckDB WASM
duckdb = import("https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@duckdb/duckdb-wasm@1.28.0/+esm")






Now we can set up our in browser DuckDB instance/connection. This is a bit more involved than the server-side version because we have to set up a web worker to run the database in a separate thread from the main browser UI thread.

// Initialize with jsDelivr bundles (recommended approach)
db = {
  const JSDELIVR_BUNDLES = duckdb.getJsDelivrBundles();
  const bundle = await duckdb.selectBundle(JSDELIVR_BUNDLES);

  const worker_url = URL.createObjectURL(
    new Blob([`importScripts("${bundle.mainWorker}");`], {type: 'text/javascript'})
  );

  const worker = new Worker(worker_url);
  const logger = new duckdb.ConsoleLogger();
  const db = new duckdb.AsyncDuckDB(logger, worker);
  
  await db.instantiate(bundle.mainModule, bundle.pthreadWorker);
  URL.revokeObjectURL(worker_url);
  
  return db;
}






Looks good. Now we can connect to the cloud data storage and run our query.

// Query S3 Parquet using HTTPS URL
wasmResult = {
  const conn = await db.connect();
  
  try {
    const result = await conn.query(`
      SELECT * 
     FROM 'https://huggingface.co/datasets/ran-codes/mtcars/resolve/refs%2Fconvert%2Fparquet/default/train/0000.parquet'  
      LIMIT 5
    `);
    
    return result.toArray().map(row => row.toJSON());
    
  } finally {
    await conn.close();
  }
}






Looks like it worked. Lets print results

wasmResult







Inputs.table(wasmResult)










Architecture Implications
Deployment Simplicity:

Build once, deploy to any static host
No server provisioning or maintenance
Automatic scaling via CDN

Cost Efficiency:

No compute costs (client-side processing)
No database hosting fees
Pay only for static hosting and data egress

Performance Characteristics:

Initial WASM load overhead (~2-3MB)
Subsequent queries run locally
Optimal for <100MB datasets per query




Appendix: CORS and Cloud Storage
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) controls browser access to cross-domain resources.
Why Hugging Face works:

CORS headers allow browser access (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *)
Optimized for ML/data science integration

For custom deployments:
S3:
[{
  "AllowedOrigins": ["https://yourapp.com"],
  "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "HEAD"], 
  "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
  "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000
}]
Azure Blob:
{
  "allowedOrigins": ["https://yourapp.com"],
  "allowedMethods": ["GET"],
  "maxAgeInSeconds": 3600
}
Security note: CORS controls browser access, not authentication. Use signed URLs or IAM policies for data security.

Caching







Term
Meaning




Target directory
Where Cargo stores build output and the state it checks to skip unchanged work (target/ by default); also called the build cache. One per workspace, so each git worktree gets its own. Similar to Next.js’s .next/ or dbt’s target/


Fresh
A unit whose cached output is up to date, so Cargo skips it


Dirty
A unit that changed, so Cargo rebuilds it


Incremental compilation
rustc reuses work from the last compile of the same crate


Cold / warm build
Informal. A build with an empty vs. populated target directory


rustc wrapper
A program Cargo runs in place of rustc (build.rustc-wrapper)


sccache
Third-party. A rustc wrapper that caches compile output across directories




Target directory layout
The subfolders that matter for build speed. deps/ and incremental/ sit inside each profile folder, not at the top of target/.







Path
Holds




target/debug/
Output of a plain cargo build; compiles fast, runs slow


target/release/
Output of cargo build --release; compiles slow, runs fast. The final files sit at its top level, like Next.js’s out/


target/<profile>/deps/
Compiled dependencies; most of a cold build, and the part sccache can share


target/<profile>/incremental/
Incremental state for your own crates; filled on the first build in each target directory. sccache does not cache incremental compiles

title: Experiment: does /clear queue in Claude Code?
section: Test 1 - does /clear wait behind running work?
text:
Test 1 - does /clear wait behind running work?

Protocol
In a scratch session:

1.1 Ask: “run python -c "import time; time.sleep(30)" in Bash, then say DONE”

not sleep 30 — the Bash tool blocks foreground sleep and backgrounds it, which ends the turn immediately and invalidates the test (attempt 1 did this)

1.2 While it sleeps, type /clear
1.3 Then type “what did I just ask you?”



Result





Test 1: question answered mid-turn, /clear still queued below


Answer: yes. /clear waited — but the typed question didn’t.



Typed mid-turn
What happened




/clear
queued until the turn ended


“what did I ask?”
answered right away, with memory



Analysis

Text mid-turn → joins the running turn
Slash command mid-turn → waits for turn end
So /clear does queue — but typed text jumps ahead of it
The “inconsistency”: /clear on an idle session fires instantly; mid-turn it waits

Gaps

Assumes /clear was typed before the question
Screenshot ends before /clear fired — did it clear after the Stop hook?

title: Experiment: does /clear queue in Claude Code?
section: Test 2 - if Claude stops to ask me something does the turn end -> does a queued /clear still wait?
text:
Test 2 - if Claude stops to ask me something does the turn end -> does a queued /clear still wait?
In a scratch session:

2.1 Ask: “run python -c "import time; time.sleep(30)" in Bash, then ask me a yes/no question with AskUserQuestion”
2.2 While it sleeps, type /clear — and nothing else
2.3 Wait for the question to appear. Note: did /clear fire at that moment, or is it still queued?

fired → a pending question counts as idle
still queued → a pending question counts as busy


Answer: no, the turn does not end. /clear waited for my answer.

After the 30s sleep, the AskUserQuestion prompt appeared and /clear stayed queued
/clear only ran after I answered the question and the turn finished
So a pending question counts as busy — the turn is paused, not over
For the /dev-log loop: a skill that stops to ask something will hold the queue, not drop it

Reflections

Things I really enjoyed
Lightweight tech stacks like these bring me great joy. You can leverage mature and developer-friendly open-science/open-source infrastructure such as GitHub Pages, Zenodo, and fully serverless application frameworks like SSG Next.js. This removes so much maintenance and operational work you have to do to maintain a deliverable and allows you to free up the time to focus on what is important: the UI of the final product and having a deep understanding of the stakeholders’ true needs.
